q: find . -name '*.txt' | xargs wc -l breaks on "My Report.txt". What fixes it?
expl: Null bytes can't appear in file names, so -print0 with -0 splits the list safely.

q: find -exec cmd {} \; versus find -exec cmd {} + — what is the difference?
expl: The plus form works like xargs and is much faster for many files.
opts: \; runs the command once per file, + passes many files at once
+ runs the command once per file, \; passes many files at once

q: You run `find . -name '*.txt' | xargs wc -l` and one file is called `My Report.txt`. What happens to that file?
expl: Plain xargs splits its input on spaces and new lines, so one name with a space becomes two missing files.
opts: xargs splits it into two names, `./My` and `Report.txt`, and wc can't find them

q: Type a command that runs `wc -l` on every `*.txt` file in the current folder and still works when a name has a space in it.
expl: `-print0` ends every name with a null byte and `xargs -0` splits on exactly that. `-exec wc -l {} +` is just as safe.

q: In the demo folder there are three `.txt` files. How many lines does this print?
expl: With `+`, find passes all three names to a single `echo`, so you get one line. With `\;` you'd get three.

q: Type a command that only PRINTS `rm --` followed by every `*.tmp` file (safe for spaces), so you can check it before deleting anything.
expl: Putting `echo` in front shows exactly what would run, and nothing is deleted. Drop the `echo` when it looks right.

q: Why does the lesson write `rm --` instead of just `rm`?
expl: Without `--`, a name that starts with a dash would be read as an option instead of a file.
opts: `--` makes rm ask before each file
`--` tells rm that no options follow, so a file named like `-v` is treated as a file

q: Type a command that gzips every `*.log` file in `logs` (some names have spaces), one file per gzip, up to 4 at a time.
expl: `-P 4` runs up to four gzips at once and `-n 1` gives each one a single file; `-print0` with `-0` keeps "app 1.log" in one piece.
`-n 1` starts one command per input item; `-P 4` decides how many of them run at the same time.
opts: Runs only one job at a time
Gives each command just one argument (one file)

expl: `-n 2` gives each `echo` at most two items, so echo runs twice.
